The sun beat down something fierce that day, and the air just hung still and thick like a quilt in a closin’ room. Dust rose up from the wagon wheels and stuck to everything, and the flies, they was everywhere, buzzing around the molasses barrel outside the general store and settling on the back of any critter that stood still too long. It was market day, and the main street was plumb full of folks from the settlements, come to trade their eggs and their furs for salt pork and new shoes, and maybe a bit of gossip too.

Right there in the middle of it all stood Silas Crum, a scrawny man with a face like a dried apple, and a voice that grated on you worse than a rusty hinge. He was holding forth to a small crowd, his arms a-waving like he was shooing chickens, telling tales about his shooting, how he could hit a fly on a pumpkin at fifty paces, and how there warn’t a squirrel in three counties that could outsmart his old rifle, named Ol’ Bess. He said he was the best shot west of the Mississippi, and he challenged any man, young or old, to come forth and prove him wrong. He even laid his last silver dollar down on the counter of Mr. Periwinkle’s store, daring anybody to match it, and I seen him puff his chest out like a turkey gobbler. Most folks just nodded and shuffled their feet, knowing Silas was more wind than skill, and they was used to his bluster.

But then Old Man Jedediah, him that owned the grist mill and never spoke much, he stepped out of the shadow of the store porch. Jedediah was a quiet sort, with eyes that saw right through you and a beard like white moss on an old oak. He didn’t say nothing, just reached into his vest pocket and laid down a dollar that looked twice as big and shiny as Silas’s. Silas’s jaw dropped a bit, but he puffed up his chest and grinned, a sly look in his eyes. “Alright, Jedediah,” he hollers, “we’ll see who’s the better man then! What’ll it be, a mark on the wall; a bottle on a fence post?” Jedediah, he just pointed a long, bony finger at a clay pot sitting on the top shelf inside Mr. Periwinkle’s store, high up and half-hidden by a sack of beans. “That there pot,” he says, his voice low and steady, “we’ll see who can shoot the hole out of the handle.”

Now that was a tiny target, and a tricky one too, for the light was bad inside the store. Silas looked mighty uncomfortable, but he’d made his boast, so he couldn’t back down now. He picked up Ol’ Bess, sighted real careful, and let fly. The bullet whizzed past, kicking up a puff of flour from a bag nearby, but the pot handle was still whole. Then Jedediah took his turn. He didn’t even raise his rifle all the way, just held it loose-like, and then a quick crack, and a tiny chip flew off the pot handle. He hadn’t shot the hole clean out, but he’d hit it, and Silas hadn't even come close. The crowd murmured, and some folks started to grin.

Silas, he went red in the face, and he snatched his dollar up from the counter. “That warn’t fair!” he squawked, “The light was bad, and you cheated somehow, you old fox!” Jedediah just looked at him, those deep eyes fixed on Silas like a hawk on a field mouse. “Cheated?” he says, and his voice warn’t loud but it carried, “I done what you challenged. You didn’t.” And then Jedediah just picked up both dollars, Silas’s and his own, and put them back in his vest pocket. He turned around slow and went back to his mill, the crowd parting for him, and I seen him give a little smile as he walked. Silas stood there, looking at the empty counter, and then at the folks who was now openly laughing at him. He tried to say something more, but his voice give out, and he just slunk away, muttering, and the sound of the laughter followed him all the way down the street till he was out of sight.

Coming up the street was the blamedest sight you ever did see. It warn’t a single person, nor even a family, but a whole procession, and a gaudy one at that. First come a big, rickety wagon, painted in all sorts of bright, clashing colors—reds and blues and yellows—and on the side it had big letters that said, “Professor Phileas Philpot’s Paragon Panacea and Perpetual Pleasure Palace!” The wagon was pulled by two scrawny mules that looked like they hadn’t had a good meal in a month of Sundays, and on the driver’s seat sat a man with a top hat too tall for his head and a handlebar mustache that twisted up like a couple of snake charmers’ pets. He was playing the banjo, not very well, but loud, and grinning from ear to ear, showing a set of teeth that looked a bit too white to be natural. Beside him, a woman with a bright red dress and a feather in her hair was beating a tambourine with a fierce joy, her eyes sparkling like she’d found a whole pocketful of diamonds. Behind the wagon walked a young fellow, tall and skinny like a scarecrow, juggling three bright-colored balls that he kept tossing higher and higher, till sometimes you thought they’d hit the eaves of the stores. He had a face that looked like it had been carved from wood, all sharp angles and solemn, but he never dropped a ball. And last, trotting along beside him, was a small, yappy dog with a ridiculously big bow tied to its ear, barking at everything and nothing, just for the sheer pleasure of making a noise.

The crowd, which had been getting restless and kinda glum after the Boggs business, and then the quiet excitement of Jedediah and Silas, it brightened up considerable. Folks started nudging each other and pointing, and a low hum of chatter went through the street. The Professor, or whatever he called himself, he seen the crowd, and he whipped the mules with his reins, and the whole contraption come to a stop right in front of the biggest store, not ten yards from where I was standing. The banjo playing got louder, and the tambourine shook like a rattlesnake’s tail, and the little dog barked fit to burst.

“Greetings, good people of this magnificent river-side metropolis!” the Professor hollers, his voice booming like a cannon, and he stands up in the wagon seat, pulling off his tall hat with a flourish. He had a head of hair that was slicked back with something shiny, and when he bowed, it caught the sunlight like a polished apple. “Professor Phileas Philpot, at your humble service, and at the service of your ailments, your ennui, and your empty pockets, which I promise to fill with mirth and marvels!”

The crowd chuckled a bit, some of them still squinting against the sun, trying to get a good look. The juggler, he kept on juggling, but he moved closer to the wagon, and the woman with the red dress, she hopped down with a spring in her step, and started to hand out little printed flyers to the folks in the front row. I got one myself, and it was covered in flowery language about the "Elixir of Eternal Youth and Unstoppable Vigor," and how it could cure everything from ingrown toenails to a broken heart, all for the low, low price of fifty cents a bottle.

“Now, I know what you’re thinking!” the Professor shouts, and he leans forward like he’s about to share a secret. “You’re thinking, ‘Another traveling show, another charlatan with a bottle of colored water and a line of honeyed words.’ And to that, I say, ‘Fie! Away with such cynicism, you skeptics of the soul!’ For I, Professor Phileas Philpot, bring you not only a remedy for the body, but a feast for the eyes and a tonic for the spirit!”

With that, he waved his hand, and the skinny juggler, who had been quiet as a church mouse, he suddenly took a big leap onto a small, wobbly platform that had been set up on the back of the wagon. He bowed deep, and then he started juggling not three balls, but five, and then six, and then he was throwing them so high they looked like little birds against the sky, and catching them without so much as a flicker in his solemn eyes. He even started doing it with one hand, and then behind his back, and the crowd let out a collective gasp, and then a ripple of applause. This warn’t no amateur show; this fellow had some real skill.

“Marvelous, ain’t it?” the Professor says, beaming, while the juggler finished his act with a flourish and a deep bow, catching all six balls at once. “And that, my friends, is but a taste of the wonders that await you! But before we delve deeper into the mysteries of the human condition, and the marvels of Professor Philpot’s Elixir, I must first present to you my lovely assistant, Miss Seraphina Sparkle, whose voice is as sweet as angels’ whispers, and whose wit is sharper than a barber’s razor!”

Miss Seraphina, she curtsies, and her red dress swirled around her, and then she picked up a small guitar from the wagon and started to pluck out a lively tune. She had a pretty voice, a bit thin, but clear, and she sang a song about a wandering heart and a moonlit night, and some of the older men in the crowd looked like they was remembering their courting days, and a few of the women even swayed a little. She finished with a flourish, and there was more applause, and a few whistles from the younger fellows.

“Now, my friends, to the main event!” the Professor announces, clapping his hands together. “You’ve seen the dexterity of Monsieur Jacques, the juggler supreme, and you’ve heard the dulcet tones of Miss Seraphina! But what good are these pleasures, if your body aches, your mind is clouded, and your very spirit feels as though it’s been dragged through a muddy swamp?”

He paused for dramatic effect, and then he picked up a dark, heavy-looking bottle from a box on the wagon. It had a fancy label with gold writing, and it looked very official. “This, my friends, is Professor Phileas Philpot’s Paragon Panacea! Distilled from the purest mountain herbs, blended with the finest river water, and blessed by the very rays of the setting sun, it is a potion unlike any other! It banishes pain, it restores vigor, it sharpens the mind, and it even, yes, it even helps a gentleman look more appealing to the fairer sex, and a lady to bloom with irresistible charm!”

He held the bottle up high, and the sun glinted off it, making it seem even more potent. A few of the older women in the crowd exchanged glances, and a couple of young men puffed out their chests a bit.

“Now, I know some of you may doubt,” the Professor continued, his voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper, “You may say, ‘Professor, these claims are too grand, too miraculous for a simple man like me to believe.’ And to that, I say, ‘Witness!’ For I have brought with me a living testament to the power of my Panacea!”

He looked around the crowd, his eyes scanning every face, and then he pointed a long, bony finger right at a grizzled old man standing near the front, a man with a stoop and a face as wrinkled as a dried apple. “You, sir! Yes, you there, with the distinguished beard and the look of wisdom in your eyes! Come forward, if you please!”

The old man, who looked a bit surprised, hesitated for a moment, and then, encouraged by a nudge from his neighbor, he shuffled forward, leaning on a cane. He looked like he was about ninety, and every step was a struggle.

“Tell these good people, my friend,” the Professor says, his voice full of sympathy, “What ails you? What burden does Father Time place upon your weary frame?”

The old man, he cleared his throat, and his voice was raspy. “Well, Professor, I got the rheumatiz in my knees somethin’ fierce. Can’t hardly walk without it shootin’ pains up my legs. And my back, it’s been bent for fifty years from working the fields. And my eyes, they ain’t what they used to be, and my memory, well, I can’t hardly remember what I had for breakfast.” He looked at the crowd, a bit embarrassed, and a few folks nodded, knowing exactly what he meant.

“A classic case!” the Professor declared, throwing his hands up in the air. “The ravages of age, the inescapable toll of toil! But fear not, for Professor Philpot’s Panacea is here!” He poured a small amount of the dark liquid from the bottle into a little silver cup and offered it to the old man. “Drink this, my friend, and feel the ancient fires of youth rekindle in your veins!”

The old man looked at the cup, then at the Professor, then at the crowd, a bit doubtful. But he took the cup, and with a gulp, he swallowed the dark liquid. He coughed a bit, and his eyes watered, and he made a face that suggested it didn’t taste like honey.

“Now, stand straight, my friend!” the Professor commanded. “Feel the warmth spreading, the aches receding! Walk, man, walk!”

The old man, he blinked a few times, and then, slowly, tentatively, he straightened his back a little. He took a step, then another, without his cane. He still looked old, mind you, and he still looked a bit shaky, but he *was* walking a little straighter, and he even managed a small, wobbly smile.

“By gum!” someone in the crowd whispered, “He’s moving better!”

“It’s a miracle!” a woman shouted, and she clapped her hands together.

The Professor, he beamed. “There you have it, folks! The power of the Panacea! A new lease on life for this venerable gentleman! Who among you wishes to banish your aches and pains? Who among you craves the vitality of youth? Step right up, my friends, and secure your bottle of Professor Phileas Philpot’s Paragon Panacea for only fifty cents! A small price for a lifetime of renewed health and boundless joy!”

And with that, Miss Seraphina and Monsieur Jacques, they jumped down from the wagon, and started circulating through the crowd with baskets full of the dark bottles, calling out the virtues of the elixir. And wouldn’t you know it, folks started reaching into their pockets. The sight of the old man walking a little straighter, even if it was just for a minute or two, it had worked its magic. People was lining up, eager to get their hands on a bottle, hoping for their own little miracle. I seen some of the folks who had been laughing at Silas earlier, they was now eagerly shelling out their hard-earned money for the Professor’s brew.

I myself, I warn’t buying it. I mean, the old man, he looked a bit better, but it could’ve just been the excitement, or maybe a strong shot of cheap whiskey in that bottle. But I stayed to watch, because it was a spectacle, and folks in these river towns, they love a good show, whether it’s a hanging or a healing.

Then, just as the selling was at its peak, and the Professor was still spouting off about the wonders of his concoction, a big, burly fellow with a red beard and a mean look in his eye pushed his way through the crowd. He was carrying an empty bottle, and he looked mighty mad.

“Hold on there, Professor!” he hollers, his voice like a bullfrog’s croak. “You call this here stuff a ‘panacea’? I bought a bottle yesterday, and all it done was give me the runs somethin’ awful! I ain’t felt this bad since I ate that bad catfish three years ago!” He waved the empty bottle in the air, sloshing a bit of liquid that was still clinging to the inside. “I want my fifty cents back, you fraud!”

The crowd went quiet all of a sudden, and all the smiles seemed to melt right off their faces. This warn’t part of the show, and you could feel the tension rise, like the steam from a hot iron. The Professor, he stopped his spiel, and he looked at the burly man, but his grin didn’t falter, not one bit.

“Ah, my good man!” the Professor says, his voice still smooth as silk. “A most interesting, and I daresay, *unusual* reaction! You see, the Paragon Panacea, it works in mysterious ways, like the very currents of this mighty river! Sometimes, before the true healing can begin, the body must first undergo a thorough cleansing, a… purification, if you will! The very toxins that have plagued your system for years, they are being purged! And a temporary… discomfort, is merely the sign that the elixir is working its marvelous magic!”

The burly man, he just stared, and he looked a bit confused by all them fancy words. “Purging? Discomfort? I just spent half the night in the privy, and I feel worse than I did before!” he roared, his face getting redder. “I want my money back!”

Miss Seraphina, she looked a little nervous, and Monsieur Jacques, he stopped trying to sell bottles and stood a little straighter, his hands ready. The little dog even stopped yapping and huddled under the wagon.

“My dear fellow, I assure you,” the Professor continued, unfazed, “what you experienced was merely the prelude to your glorious rebirth! Think of it as a river overflowing its banks before settling into a new, cleaner channel! Why, in a few days, you will feel so invigorated, so renewed, you will thank me for this temporary inconvenience!” He reached into his coat pocket, and pulled out a small, folded piece of paper. “In fact, for your courage in undergoing such a profound detoxification, I offer you a special certificate for a free second bottle, a testament to your body’s remarkable capacity for renewal!”

He held out the certificate with a grand gesture. The burly man, he looked at the certificate, then at the Professor’s smiling face, then at the crowd, which was still quiet, waiting to see what would happen. He seemed torn, between his anger and the promise of a free bottle, even if the first one had made him sick.

“A free bottle, you say?” the burly man grumbled, a bit of the fight going out of him.

“Indeed, a token of my profound admiration for your robust constitution!” the Professor replied, with a low bow. “Come, let me personally select the very finest elixir for your continued journey to unparalleled health!”

The burly man, after a moment of glaring, snatched the certificate, and then, surprisingly, he followed the Professor to the back of the wagon, where the Professor made a show of picking out a bottle with extra care, holding it up to the light and murmuring about its potency. The crowd, they let out a collective sigh of relief, and a few people even chuckled at the way the Professor had talked himself out of trouble. It seemed the showmanship was just as important as the medicine.

After that little incident, the selling picked up again, though a bit slower this time. The Professor started telling stories about all the incredible cures his Panacea had brought about, tales of blind men seeing, deaf men hearing, and cripples throwing away their crutches. He even claimed it once brought a dead mule back to life, though he admitted that was a particularly potent batch. He talked and talked, till the sun was really starting to beat down hard, and the dust was getting thick from all the comings and goings.

I seen a few more people buy bottles, mostly the ones who looked like they had a long list of complaints already. And then, just as the Professor was winding down, and saying his farewells, and getting ready to move his colorful wagon on to the next town, a young mother with a sickly-looking baby in her arms pushed her way through to the front. Her face was pale, and her eyes were red from crying.

“Professor, please!” she pleads, her voice trembling. “My baby, he’s got the fever somethin’ terrible. He won’t eat, he just cries all day and night. The local doctor, he says there ain’t much hope. Can your Panacea, can it help him?”

The crowd went silent again, and all eyes turned to the Professor. This warn’t like the old man’s rheumatiz, or the burly man’s upset stomach. This was a tiny, innocent child, and the mother’s desperation was plain for all to see.

The Professor, his usual beaming smile, it faltered for a second, just a flicker. He looked at the pale baby, then at the mother’s tear-stained face, and for the first time, he looked less like a showman and more like a man who might be caught in a lie.

He cleared his throat, and his voice, for the first time, wasn’t booming. “My dear woman,” he says, and he actually sounds a bit unsure, “the Paragon Panacea, it is a powerful tonic, meant for adults, to restore their vigor and health. For a babe so young, so delicate… I cannot say. It is not designed for such tender systems.”

The mother’s face fell, and she looked like she was about to burst into fresh tears. The crowd murmured, some shaking their heads, some looking at the Professor with a new, harder expression.

Then, Miss Seraphina, the woman in the red dress, she stepped forward. She put a hand on the mother’s shoulder. “Professor,” she says, and her voice was soft but firm, “We carry a special blend, a soothing syrup for infants, made from the gentlest of herbs. It is not the Panacea, but it has brought comfort to many a fretful child.”

The Professor looked at her, a moment of surprise on his face, but then he quickly nodded. “Ah, yes, my dear Seraphina is quite right! My apologies, madam, my mind was so focused on the universal applications of the Panacea, I forgot our specialized infant cordial! It is a milder remedy, specially formulated for the little ones!”

He pulled out another, smaller bottle, with a different label, from a separate box. This one had a picture of a smiling baby on it, which seemed a bit unlikely. “This, my dear, is the ‘Cradle Calm Cordial.’ It will soothe your baby’s fever, ease his discomfort, and bring him peaceful sleep.” He handed it to the mother. “And for you, my dear, because a mother’s heart is the greatest panacea of all, this bottle is on the house.”

The mother looked at the smaller bottle, and then at the Professor’s face, and a tiny glimmer of hope returned to her eyes. “Oh, thank you, Professor! Thank you, Miss Seraphina! May God bless you both!” she cried, and she clutched the bottle to her chest, and then she turned and hurried away, back into the crowd.

The Professor, he watched her go, and he didn’t put on his usual big smile right away. He stood there for a moment, looking a bit thoughtful, and then he let out a big breath. Miss Seraphina, she gave him a small, knowing look, and he gave her a quick nod.

Then, with a clap of his hands, he was back in full showman mode. “And that, my friends, concludes our humble presentation for today! Remember, Professor Phileas Philpot’s Paragon Panacea is not just a cure, it’s a promise! A promise of health, happiness, and a brighter tomorrow!” He jumped back onto the driver’s seat. “We must now bid you farewell, for the open road calls, and other towns yearn for the wonders of the Panacea!”

He cracked the whip over the mules’ heads, and with a creak and a groan, the rickety wagon started to roll again. The banjo struck up a lively tune, and Miss Seraphina beat her tambourine, and Monsieur Jacques started juggling his balls again, tossing them higher than ever as they went down the street. The little dog yapped excitedly, running alongside the wagon.

The crowd watched them go, some still holding their newly purchased bottles, some shaking their heads, and some just looking thoughtful. The whole incident with the baby seemed to have put a different flavor on the performance, even for me. It showed a flicker of something real, a brief moment where the showman nearly faltered, and then was saved by his assistant’s quick thinking, and maybe a touch of genuine human feeling, mixed in with the usual hocus pocus.

As the wagon disappeared down the street, and the sounds of the banjo and tambourine faded, the quiet settled back on the town, but it was a different kind of quiet now. It warn’t the expectant quiet from before, nor the tense quiet after the Sherburn shooting. It was a kind of weary quiet, like folks had seen a whole lot in one day, and their emotions had been stretched and pulled in too many directions.

The sun was lower now, painting the sky with streaks of orange and purple, and a cooler breeze was starting to blow in from the river, carrying the smell of mud and wet wood. People started to break up, heading towards their homes, or maybe to the saloon for a drink to settle their nerves. The market vendors started packing up their wares, and the wagons that had brought families in from the country were slowly rumbling out of town.

I stood there for a spell, just watching the last of the crowds thin out. It had been a day, alright. From Boggs getting shot, to the lynching talk, to Jedediah besting Silas, and now this medicine show, it had been a full measure of human nature, all squeezed into a few short hours. It made you think, it really did. About how easily people could be swayed, by anger, by amusement, by the promise of a miracle. And how quick a good showman could turn a bad situation into a new opportunity.

I decided I’d better head back to the steamboat. The day was done, and I reckoned I’d seen enough excitement to last me a week. As I walked along the dusty street, I passed by the spot where Boggs had fallen, and where the lanky man had reenacted the shooting. There warn’t nothing there now but trampled dust, but I could still see it in my mind’s eye, plain as day. The way Boggs had thrown up his hands, the two bangs, and then him tumbling backwards. And the girl, his daughter, screaming. It was a sight that stuck with you, like a burr under your saddle.

I also remembered the little girl with the sickly baby, and the way the Professor had given her the cordial for free. I’ll be dancin’ with my missus at the next county fair, I will!” And he stomped his foot down, not a fancy jig like Withers, but a good, solid stomp, and you could see the wonder in his eyes.

I watched all this from the edge of the crowd, keeping a keen eye on the Professor and his boys, and on the folks buying the stuff. I seen how quick the money was changing hands, and how the Professor, he had a way of looking folks right in the eye, and making them believe every word he said, even if his words was as slippery as a greased pig. He had a look that promised a whole lot, and folks, they was eager to buy into that promise. He was a master, I tell you, a regular ringleader of dreams, and he had that whole town in the palm of his hand. I reckon he could’ve sold them swampland in Florida and they’d have bought it too, just for a chance to feel like Man Withers.

The sun was getting hotter, beating down on the street, and the dust was rising from all the commotion, making a hazy cloud around the Professor’s wagon. The two young fellers selling the bottles, their shirts was getting damp with sweat, but they kept a-going, never slowing down, their hands moving like a pair of pistons, grabbing money, handing out bottles, their faces set in a sort of eager, determined way. They must have sold a hundred bottles in a quarter of an hour, easy. And the Professor, he just kept talking, spinning his yarns about the ancient secrets, and the powerful herbs, and the pure mountain springs where his elixir was brewed.

“This, my friends, is no ordinary tonic! This is the very breath of the ancient mountains, bottled for your rejuvenation! It cures the rheum, the aches, the pains, the coughs, the fevers, the weak eyes, the failing memory, the lack of vim and vigor, and even, yes, even the melancholy of the spirit!” he proclaimed, gesturing grandly with his hands, his voice reaching a crescendo, and the crowd, they hung on his every word, their faces uplifted, their mouths a little open, like little birds waiting for a worm. He had them right where he wanted them, hooked and reeled in, and I reckoned they’d be buying anything he had to sell for the rest of the day.

Man Withers, he was still prancing about a bit, though maybe not quite so high as before, and he was telling anybody who’d listen about how his joints felt like new, and how his eyesight, which had been failing him for years, was suddenly keen as a hawk’s. He was a powerful advertisement, he was, and the Professor knew it too, because every now and then he’d point to Withers and say, “There, my friends, is living proof! Living, breathing, dancing proof of the miraculous power of Professor Dulce’s Grand Elixir of Life!”

A woman with a pale, sickly-looking boy, no older than ten, she pushed her way to the front, her face drawn with worry. “Professor, sir,” she says, her voice trembling a bit, “my little Johnny, he’s been ailing for nigh on a year, a fever that just won’t break, and he’s thin as a rail. Do you reckon your elixir could help him?”

The Professor, he stopped his speech right then, and he leaned down, looking at the boy with a look that was full of deep concern, like he was the boy’s own father. “My dear woman,” he says, his voice softer now, almost mournful, “it grieves my heart to see such a tender bloom withering before its time. Bring him here, let the Elixir of Life touch his lips, and watch the color return to his cheeks, the sparkle to his eyes!”

The mother, she practically shoved the boy forward, her hands shaking as she pulled a crumpled wad of bills from her apron pocket. The Professor himself took a fresh bottle, uncorked it with a flourish, and held it to the boy’s lips, gently tipping it so a small amount trickled down his throat. The boy coughed, made a face, but then he looked up, and for a moment, a tiny flicker of something like energy seemed to pass through his small frame. His eyes, they seemed a bit brighter, and he let out a small, weak sigh.

“He breathes easier, Professor,” the mother whispered, tears welling in her eyes, “he breathes easier!” And she fell to her knees right there, clutching the boy, her heart full of gratitude. The crowd, they murmured in awe, and some of the women, they started to sniffle, touched by the sight.

I seen the Professor, he just give a little nod, a solemn, respectful nod, and then he rose and looked out at the crowd, and his voice, it gained a new power, a sort of holy fervor. “See, my friends, the very young, too, are blessed by its touch! The Elixir, it knows no age, no ailment, no barrier it cannot overcome! It purifies the blood, strengthens the heart, invigorates the limbs, and brings joy back to the sorrowful soul! Buy now, while supplies last! For this day, this glorious day, will soon pass, and with it, perhaps, your only chance at true renewal!”

The sales, they picked up again with renewed frenzy. Folks was buying two, three bottles at a time, some for themselves, some for ailing relatives who couldn’t make it to town. The young fellers was barely keeping up, their faces red with exertion and the heat. The Professor, he was a regular general, directing his troops, his eyes scanning the crowd, always finding the next eager customer, always having the right word, the right gesture, to keep the money flowing.

I started to get a bit fidgety, watching all this. It was a grand show, no doubt about it, and the Professor, he was a first-class showman, better than most medicine men I’d seen, and I’d seen a fair few in my travels. But there was something about it that just didn’t sit right, a kind of hollowness behind all the grand promises. It was too easy, too neat, like a story that was all wrapped up with a shiny bow, but you knew there was a snag in the thread if you just looked close enough.

But I noticed his jig wasn’t quite so high anymore, and his voice, it had lost a little of that booming quality, and was beginning to sound a mite raspy, like it had before. He wasn’t whooping and yelling now, just talking, and I seen him lean a bit on his cane, which he’d picked up again, though he was still swinging it around a bit for emphasis. His smile, it wasn’t quite so wide, and his eyes, they was beginning to lose that shine, getting a bit cloudy, like the morning mist.

It was subtle, at first, so subtle you wouldn’t notice it if you wasn’t paying keen attention, like I was. But the change was there. The bounce was going out of his step, and the spring was going out of his back. He was beginning to look a bit tired, a bit worn, just like he had before he took that gulp of the Professor’s elixir.

The cronies, they exchanged glances, but they didn’t say nothing, just nodded vaguely.

He hadn’t noticed the change in Withers, or if he had, he was mighty good at pretending he hadn’t. He was a clever one, that Professor, and he knew how to keep a crowd’s attention. He was telling them a tale now, a grand, fantastical tale about a hidden spring in the Rocky Mountains, guarded by ancient spirits, and how only he, the Professor, with his years of scholarly study and perilous journeys, had been able to discover its secrets and harness its life-giving waters for the benefit of mankind.

“And it is not just the body, my friends, that finds renewal in this sacred draught!” he cried, his voice dropping to a conspiratorial whisper, but still loud enough for all to hear. “No, it is the mind, the very soul, that is uplifted! Your thoughts shall be clearer, your worries banished, your spirit soaring free, like an eagle above the highest peak! For what is the body without a vigorous mind, a joyful heart?
